messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Vignette:
Kwame is a 62-year-old African American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a bomb disposal technician, a role in which vigilance, procedure, and respect for hidden danger had long felt like strengths rather than burdens. He is married and had taken pride in being the person others relied on in high-risk situations. The event he returns to when he begins describing why he is now seeking help happened at work during what was supposed to be a controlled response to a hazardous device that turned out to involve toxic chemical exposure. He remembers the site not as a blur but as a sequence of sensory details that still feel dangerously immediate: the sealed gear, the tension of approaching the device, the abrupt noise when the situation changed, and then the sharp, invasive smell of chemicals as the area was breached. In the aftermath there were emergency protocols, decontamination, and medical evaluation, all accompanied by the sterile smell of antiseptic and hospital cleaning fluids. What stayed with him was not only the fear that he had been exposed to something lethal, but the sense that danger could be present in the air itself, invisible and already inside his body before he could stop it.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame found that being back in the workplace carried a charge he had not expected. Entering the building, stepping into operational areas, or hearing the familiar sounds of the job no longer felt routine. Loud noises were especially difficult. A slammed metal door, equipment clattering, or any sudden bang could snap his body into alarm before he had time to think. He described reacting as if something catastrophic were happening again. Hospital and antiseptic smells were just as potent. Passing a clinic corridor, catching the scent of disinfectant, or even being near ambulance bays could abruptly return him to those hours after the exposure, when he had felt trapped between contamination and uncertainty.

Over time, Kwame began organizing his life around not feeling caught off guard. Wherever he went, he identified exits first and did not really settle until he knew how he could get out. In restaurants, waiting rooms, church, and at work, his eyes moved across doors, hallways, and possible barriers almost automatically. He was constantly scanning for signs that something was wrong in the environment, watching people, sounds, and movement around him with the same intensity he once reserved for active operations. If someone touched him unexpectedly, even lightly on the shoulder, he reacted with visible alarm. His wife came to notice that he would jerk, turn sharply, or stiffen before recognizing who was there. He found this embarrassing, but he also felt certain that letting his guard down would be reckless.

Being alone became particularly hard for him. He avoided sitting by himself in a room or staying alone in a building because solitude made him feel too exposed to his own thoughts and too far from help if something went wrong. If his wife went out, he often found reasons to leave the house as well or to keep moving from room to room rather than settle. He worked excessively, taking on more time and more tasks than he needed to, because being occupied at work felt more manageable than being alone with the memory of the exposure and the fear it still carried. This overwork had consequences. At home, his wife experienced him as present but unavailable, exhausted and preoccupied. At work, the place where he once felt most competent had also become one of his clearest triggers, leaving him caught between wanting the structure of the job and bracing himself the entire time he was there.

Medical settings became something he increasingly avoided. He did not want to go near hospitals, ambulances, or physical examinations unless absolutely necessary. The antiseptic smell alone was enough to make his chest tighten and his attention narrow. He told himself he was better off not putting himself through that unless there was no choice. Even routine care became something to postpone. To him, those places were not neutral; they were bound up with the moment when the exposure became real and when he understood that the threat was not fully under his control.

By the time he came for help, these patterns had become hard to ignore. What finally pushed him to seek treatment was not a single new event but the accumulation of strain: the constant watchfulness, the difficulty tolerating being alone, the way sudden sounds and unexpected touch still jolted him, and the fact that both work and medical care had become settings he endured rather than trusted. Kwame speaks about all of this with a mixture of discipline and fatigue. He wants relief, but he is also afraid of what it would mean to stop scanning, stop planning exits, or stop filling every quiet moment with work. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to remain in a room without first calculating how to escape it, to walk into necessary medical settings without feeling transported back to the exposure, and to be at home with his wife without feeling that stillness itself is unsafe.
